# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

This file is `references/conventions.md` in the work plugin's own folder. From
a skill's `SKILL.md` it is two folders up: `skills/work-on/SKILL.md` and
`references/conventions.md` share the plugin folder. In Codex the plugin
folder is the installed copy, for example
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command.
  Do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a pipe, or a redirect. Codex matches its
  command rule against the plain command.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Run each one
  alone, as its own command.
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. Report it that way.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The file holds the same text the
  read printed for that heading, with your changes.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --section "<heading>"
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file <file>
  ```

- To add one row to a table section (Open Questions, Recent History), use
  `--append-row` with the full Markdown table row. A new question takes the
  next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions section first and add one to
  the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is none).

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |"
  ```

- Frontmatter values change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`,
  `design`, `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. Never edit frontmatter by hand.
- A new title is the owner's call: say the new title to him in one line
  before `toolkit work set <id> --title`, and never retitle an item quietly.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or
  `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The hooks refuse it.
- Text for `--set-file` and `--body-file`:
  - Claude Code: pass it on standard input, so no file is left anywhere:
    `toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file - <<'EOF'`, then
    the text, then `EOF`.
  - Codex (and whenever a file is easier): make a new folder for this one save
    with `mktemp -d` (its name is unique, so two sessions or two projects never
    share a file), write the file in it, run the `toolkit` command alone with
    the file's full path, and after the command succeeds delete the file and
    the folder (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`). Never use a fixed name
    such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`: every project starts at `WI-001`, so
    another session's save could land in this item.
  - Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
    file there confuses the design lookup.
- Never write a work item record from the shell (`cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`,
  `cp`, or a script) and never change its frontmatter with a file edit. The
  hooks refuse both, because they would skip the approval gates.

## Section names in `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` uses. Every tracker uses the same body: the
project's `.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`, copied from the model
project.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | Phases `P1`, `P2` with Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | Tasks `P1-T01` with Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: change or decision, effect on the work |
| `Open Questions` | `Q-01` rows: question, affects, status, decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status, Starting request, Agreed goal, Active requirements `R-01`, Acceptance |
| `Notes` | Decisions and context, Resume here, Solution options and considerations |

The frontmatter fields are `id`, `title`, `type`, `stage`, `status`, `parent`,
`waiting_on`, `priority`, `delivery`, `requirements_approved`, `design`,
`result_approved`, and `updated`. Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

## Section names in `DESIGN.md`

The design has one shape in every tracker (`DESIGN.md` beside a local item,
the "Solution Design" page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub
or Jira). The CLI writes its frontmatter: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, and the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C) with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage (Build or reuse, Why it meets the requirement, How to check it), Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow, Components and responsibilities, Data, access, and integration details, Edge cases and failure behavior, Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep the headings exactly as the template has them, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

- Check the item and memory before asking the owner a question again.
- When sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Do not pick the
  convenient answer.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.

## Reporting a failed save

- A write failed: lead with "Not saved", name what was not saved and where it
  should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified".
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## When to add a history note

Add one `toolkit work history <id> --note "<text>"` when:

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you
  checked it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

Record the owner's meaning briefly. Do not add reasons, scope, or certainty he
did not give. Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs,
or small edits.

## Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask the owner for an approval or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because the
  owner just answered. After the approval, set it to `agent` when the agent
  continues. After the owner answers his last open question on the item, set
  it back the same way: `agent` when the agent can continue, `none` when
  nothing waits. Keep `owner` only while another question for him on that
  item is still open.

  ```text
  toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent
  ```

- An item left at `owner` stays in the briefing and in
  `toolkit work decisions`, and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of
  its next stage.

## Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`, for example "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in. Work it out from the record.
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item is waiting for.
  Blocked is not a status.

## Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move a folder, drag a Notion card,
change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, adds a "Changed by hand" history row,
and reports it. Never undo it. When a hand change skips a gate (a build item
moved past stage 03 without approved requirements, or Done without a recorded
result approval), ask the owner about it as a question.

The session briefing lists these changes under "Changes found in the
tracker", and every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the
owner each one in one line ("You renamed WI-002's folder to help-option; I'll
use the new path.") before other work, and add one history note on each item
whose parent or place changed.

## Branches and worktrees

- An item's code work happens in its own worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`, the form the project's
  `shared-repository-work.md` rule uses:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`.
  The briefing ties a worktree to its item by the item id in the branch name.
  With another id prefix, use it in lower case (`acme-007-...`).
- Never commit `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. They are Git-ignored and live in
  the main checkout.
- No AI credit anywhere: not in commits, pull requests, comments, or files.
- Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so `git add`, `git commit`,
  `git worktree add` and `remove`, `git merge`, `git branch -d`, `git fetch`,
  and `git push` cannot run inside it. The project's
  `.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one; a
  command he approves runs outside the sandbox. Tell him in one line what the
  command does before Codex asks. Never work around it: no nested
  `git clone` of the project, no copy of `.git/`, no building on the default
  branch instead of the item's branch.
# Closing a work item

Detail for `work-finish`. Carried over from Toolkit V1's "Finish or
cancel" rules and its "Closing a work item" checklist, with V2 homes.

## Before Done

- Give the owner a short result, the known gaps, and the evidence, and ask
  for approval. A clear earlier approval of that same result counts.
- Never describe an unverified result as complete.
- Done means the owner accepted the result. Cancelled means the work stopped
  without it.

## The pull request (stage 12)

- Push the item's branch (`claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`). Never force-push.
- Write the pull request title and description in plain words: what changed,
  why, how it was checked, and the item id. Run the description through the
  `unslop` skill, because it is read by other people. No line crediting an AI.
- Merge only through `merge-and-clean-up`, and only when one of these holds:
  - the owner said yes to this merge; or
  - `DECISIONS.md` records a standing merge instruction from the owner (the
    project's `AGENTS.md` names it there), and an `acceptance-checker` that
    did not build the change reported no blocking issue on that exact head
    commit, and every check passes. `merge-and-clean-up` step 2 checks the
    same record.
- A work item that says its merge needs the owner's approval overrides a
  standing instruction.

## Deployment (stage 13)

- Only when the result must be put somewhere beyond the default branch.
- Salesforce projects, in order: `sf-component-tracker` is current and the
  item's folder `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/` holds its
  `package.xml`, `destructiveChanges.xml` when something is removed,
  `manual-steps.md`, and `DEPLOYMENT-RECORD.md`; `sf-deploy-check` finds
  nothing that would ship too early; then a validate against the sandbox. A
  production deploy is handed to the owner: the exact command, what it
  deploys, and what to check afterwards. A release of several items uses a
  copy of `delivery/deployment/release-cutover-template/`.
- Production data changes go through `sf-data-change`, which builds the
  owner's package. The owner runs it.
- Record the owner's report of the deploy in a history note.

## Requirements baseline (stage 14)

- The work item holds the proposed requirements while the work is in
  progress. After delivery and approval, copy the delivered rules into the
  area's file in `requirements/`. Read `requirements/AGENTS.md` first. A new
  area starts as a copy of `requirements/system-area-template/`, with the
  folder and the file renamed for the business area, as the template's
  fill-in guide says. Rules that apply across areas go in
  `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md`.
- Copy only behavior that was delivered and approved. Behavior that was
  approved but not delivered is never written as shipped.
- Link the work item id from the area file when it explains a requirement,
  and add a line to its Change history. Do not copy task history there.
- When the change altered the verified structure of the current system, also
  update the area's file in `system-guide/` (a new area starts from
  `system-guide/AREA-TEMPLATE.md`), with the observed facts and the date
  checked.
- Save these files with the `publish-docs` skill (it commits and pushes the
  documents from its own worktree).
- Confirm the item links to the requirements, decisions, and code that
  actually exist. Do not create missing documents just to complete a
  checklist.

## Sub-items

- List the open sub-items before finishing a parent. Each one is finished or
  cancelled on its own (with its own approval or reason), or moved when the
  owner asks. A parent with open sub-items is finished only when the owner
  says so: then `toolkit work finish` needs `--allow-open-sub-items`
  (without it the command refuses with exit code 2), and a history note
  quotes his words.
- Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.
- Cancelling a parent: ask what happens to each open sub-item (cancel it,
  move it to the top level, or move it under another item). Never cancel them
  without asking.

## Memory

- At most one `event` record through `memory-save`, only when the episode
  will matter later, for example a costly fix or a surprising platform limit.
- Take the item off the current focus "Now" list and update its "Last
  updated" line. The focus holds work item ids only, never their status.

## Done

- `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence "<what shows it works>"`.
  The evidence names the test result, the pull request or commit, or what the
  owner saw.
- Repository work: say whether the work reached the default branch.
- Leave the folder where it is. Moving or archiving happens only on the
  owner's request, through `work-organize`.

## Cancel

- `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason "<owner's words>"`. The reason is his
  words, not a summary.
- Cancelling keeps the record. Nothing is deleted.

description: 'Starts, continues, or logs project work: finds or creates the work item, works out where it stands, and runs its next step through to a built result. Use when the owner asks to build, add, fix, or change something, says "keep going" or "continue", names an item, or wants an idea logged for later.'

# Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` (saving, section edits, history, branches) and `references/trackers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. No session briefing in this conversation: run the command below. Exit code 4 (no `.toolkit.json`): open `project-setup` and stop. When the briefing or a `toolkit work` command lists changes found in the tracker (a moved or renamed folder, a new parent, a missing item), tell the owner each one in one line before other work.
   `toolkit brief`
2. Find the item: the id the owner named, or a title in the list that matches the request. Two possible matches: ask one question naming both. No match: it is new. When `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` names the item, read its phase there too.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work list`
3. Size a new request. A quick edit (one sitting, no choice for the owner, no behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production): do it and report it, with no item. "Later", "backlog", "park that": check the list for a duplicate, create the item, write the owner's words unchanged into Starting request, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop. Anything else: create it the same way and continue.
   `toolkit work new --title "<title>" --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Starting request" --set-file <file>`
4. A substantial goal whose item shows `delivery: not-offered`: open `work-delegate` first. Quick questions and small edits get no offer.
5. Route by where the item stands, using the item and the "Continue with" column of the lifecycle. Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load` (or the risk calls for it): `work-requirements`. More than one reasonable way to build it and no approved design: `solution-design`. A `build` item going to planning without a design: say so to the owner in one line before building ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me."), and put the reason in a history note. Too big for one build: `work-organize`. Stages 09 to 11: `work-check`. Stages 12 to 14: `work-finish`. `waiting_on: owner`: ask that one question first (`work-decide`) and keep working on anything it does not block. Say the route in one line ("WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements; opening work-requirements."). Never ask the owner which stage it is in.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
6. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases `P1`, `P2` and tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) from the design's "Build and verification plan", in the format in `references/planning.md`. Tracking setup (stage 07) only when needed: the item's worktree `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on branch `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`; in a Salesforce project, the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` through `sf-component-tracker`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
7. Build (stage 08) on the item's own branch and worktree, never on the default branch. In Codex, `git worktree add`, `git add`, and `git commit` need the owner's approval, because the sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only: say in one line what each does before Codex asks, and never work around it (the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, "Branches and worktrees"). With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, and validation is clean.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "<what changed>"`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `builder`: one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed to one. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task.
- `researcher`: one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker`: a plan check after step 6, before the build, when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's "Build and verification plan", the Roadmap, and the Tasks, and ask for a plan check.
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Sizing a request

- **Quick edit, no item:** one sitting, no decision for the owner, and it does not change behavior recorded in `requirements/`. Examples: fix a typo, rename a variable, answer a question. Report what changed in one line.
- **Log only:** the owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or "log a bug". Create the item at `01-discovery`, fill Starting request with his exact words, and stop. Do not start the work.
- **Work item:** everything else. A request that grows past a quick edit while you work on it becomes an item then, with the owner's words as the Starting request.
- Types: pick the closest from the lifecycle's type list. `build` and `data-load` need approved requirements before stage 03 is passed; the CLI refuses otherwise. A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`), or to anything bound for production is `build` (data changes are `data-load`), never `task`, even when it looks small.

## Routing notes

- The lifecycle's "Continue with" column is the default. The item's real state decides: for example, a `task` type item with no open choices can skip requirements approval and go straight to planning, with the reason in a history note.
- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a short reason when a move is not obvious.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`) belongs to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Several items at once: recommend what can proceed independently, what depends on another outcome, and which decision would unblock the most work. See `references/planning.md`.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized work units, each naming its work item ID; item detail stays in the tracker. # Merge and clean up

Land one exact pull request, prove it merged, then remove only the workspace
that belonged to it. Merge and cleanup are one guarded workflow.

1. **Resolve the exact pull request** and map branches to worktrees. The local
   head branch must be at the pull request's head commit.
2. **Check the merge is allowed:** the owner's yes for this pull request, or a
   standing merge instruction recorded in `DECISIONS.md`.
3. **Preflight on GitHub:** open, not a draft, mergeable, reviews satisfied,
   required checks passed. "No checks reported" is not a failure.
4. **Merge-safety check:** after a fetch, compare
   `git diff --name-only origin/<default>...<branch>` with `git status` in the
   primary checkout. A file in both lists: stop and name it.
5. **Merge** with `gh pr merge <n> --squash --delete-branch` (no admin flags),
   then confirm the state is `MERGED`.
6. **Fast-forward the base checkout**, then remove only this pull request's

7. **Add one history note** to the linked work item. Stage moves and Done stay

   result.

  required checks, merge method, and who may merge.
- Never merge a draft, bypass branch protection, use an admin override,

resolve it from the current checkout:

```bash
git status -sb

git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
gh pr view --json number,url,state,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isCrossRepository,title,body
```

head commit, base branch, the worktree holding the head branch (if any), the

name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in project memory, and sends anything that belongs elsewhere to its home. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "always do X", "never do X", "forget that", or "remind me", corrects the agent, or a hook says to save.'
---

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line. In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a heredoc) or run from a script runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion: run it alone. Text for `--body-file` and `--set-file`: in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--set-file -` or `--body-file -` with a heredoc); in Codex make a new folder for each save with `mktemp -d`, write the file there, and delete the file and the folder after the command succeeds. Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`: another session could write the same file.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate.
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. There is no proposal inbox: keep an unanswered question in the conversation and go on with other work.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body file with the model's labels: Remember, Why, How to apply, Evidence and limits (the source and an absolute date), Related memories (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), Authoritative records. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26" or "requirements/billing.md, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. Giving the same record a better name, or a type that matches its content: rename it; links to it are repaired. Use the first save form when the owner approved (his words or his yes); the second only for a routine save in `trusted` mode.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>" --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>"`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus, change it, write it back. The model's format: a "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status. On a new project the focus still holds the setup text: remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Declined saves

- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`
